content: The following groups were identified in the survey, with participants selecting all applicable options: 41% of respondents (n=83) did not identify with any of the listed groups. 23% (n=47) identified as people living with hepatitis C. 21% (n=42) identified as people who formerly injected drugs. 18% (n=37) identified as people who currently inject drugs. 18% (n=37) selected Other and provided specific details. 16% (n=32) identified as people living with HIV. 8% (n=16) identified as partners of someone belonging to one of the above groups. 7% (n=14) identified as men who have sex with men. 6% (n=13) identified as people previously in prison. 5% (n=11) identified as sex workers. 2% (n=5) identified as migrants. Regarding hepatitis C testing and treatment: 72% of respondents (n=150) reported having been tested for hepatitis C, of whom 42% (n=60) tested positive. Among the 56 respondents who provided information about hepatitis C treatment, 91% (n=51) were either currently being treated or had previously been treated for hepatitis C. When asked about the location of their last hepatitis C test (n=142): 24% were tested at a hospital. 20% were tested at a primary care (general public) clinic. 15% were tested at a laboratory. 13% were tested at a community-based organization center. 8% were tested at a hospital outpatient department. 8% selected Other and provided specific details. 5% were tested at a drug user support center. 2% were tested at a sexual and reproductive health clinic. 2% were tested at an outreach mobile or testing camp. 1% were tested at an HIV clinic. 1% were tested at a hospital inpatient department. When asked where they would prefer to be tested for hepatitis C (n=133): 44% preferred a community-based organization center. 35% preferred a place of their choice using a self-test. 28% preferred a hospital. 28% preferred a primary care (general public) clinic. When all participants (n=184) were asked about their preferred testing location: 40% preferred a community-based organization center. 33% preferred a place of their choice using a self-test. 33% preferred a hospital. 32% preferred a primary care (general public) clinic. 29% preferred a laboratory. 23% preferred a drug user support center. 14% preferred sexual and reproductive health clinics. 11% preferred a pharmacy. 7% had no preference. 5% selected Other and provided specific details. 5% preferred an HIV clinic. Among people who inject drugs (current or former, n=54), preferences for testing locations were as follows: 54% preferred a community-based organization center. 50% preferred a drug user support center. 39% preferred self-testing. This group showed a strong preference for decentralized services, with traditional healthcare settings not featuring in their top three preferences. Regarding hepatitis C treatment: Among participants who had been treated for hepatitis C (n=45): 64% received treatment at a hospital. 22% received treatment at a primary care (general public) clinic. 7% received treatment at a drug user support center. 4% received treatment at a community-based organization center. 2% received treatment at an HIV clinic. None reported receiving treatment at a sexual and reproductive health clinic. When asked where they would prefer to receive treatment (n=175): 54% preferred the same site as their testing location. 50% preferred a community-based organization center. 39% preferred a hospital. 29% preferred a general practitioner’s office. 21% preferred a drug user support center. 10% preferred sexual and reproductive health clinics. 8% preferred an HIV clinic. 7% selected Other and provided specific details. 5% had no preference. Among people who inject drugs (current or former, n=54), preferences for treatment locations were as follows: 46% preferred a drug user support center, which was higher than the preference for this site among all respondents (21%). Key considerations for hepatitis C testing and treatment locations: The most important factor for both testing and treatment was proximity to home or office (testing: 53%; treatment: 56%). Direct costs were the second most important factor (testing: 38%; treatment: 40%). A non-judgmental and non-stigmatizing atmosphere was the third most important factor (testing: 37%; treatment: 39%). For certain populations, such as people who inject drugs and people living with HIV, a non-judgmental and non-stigmatizing atmosphere was the most important consideration. When asked if they would like to be tested and treated in the same place (n=172): 91% responded yes. The main reasons for this preference were convenience (34%) and continued follow-up from testing to treatment (33%). Preferences for discussing health needs related to hepatitis C (n=166): 48% preferred to discuss with a specialist doctor. 23% preferred community-friendly medical personnel. 11% preferred a general practitioner. 10% preferred a community or peer worker. Preferences for who should perform hepatitis C testing (n=165): 26% preferred a specialist doctor. 22% preferred a trained community or peer worker. 18% preferred community-friendly medical personnel. 10% preferred a general practitioner. 10% preferred a trained nurse. Key messages: The knowledge and expertise of trained medical professionals are highly valued, but so are the contributions of trained peer and community workers, as well as community-friendly medical personnel. A range of testing and treatment options is necessary to meet the diverse needs of different populations and ensure efficient and effective care. Limitations of the survey: The sampling method and small sample size limit the generalizability of the results. Online surveys may not reach populations without regular internet access, such as those who are homeless or marginalized. Most participants lived in urban areas, which may reduce the impact of centralized care on their responses. The survey was only available in English, potentially excluding non-Anglophone participants. Limited piloting of the survey due to time constraints may have affected its comprehensiveness.
